title: A Macroeconomic Approach to Measure US Returns from Slowing Biological Aging
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, Abundance Institute and University of South Carolina - Moore School of Business - Department of Economics

detail.title: A Macroeconomic Approach to Measure US Returns from Slowing Biological Aging
detail.abstract: Biological aging imposes significant socio-economic costs, increasing health expenses, reducing productivity, stalling population growth and straining social systems, culminating in reduced economic activity. We draw insights from interviews with 102 scientists working on aging biology and use these as the basis for four macroeconomic simulations: slowing brain aging, slowing reproductive aging, and an overall delay in biological aging (including the novel concept of “replacing aging”). Our model is calibrated to represent how slowing biological aging manifests in the US economy and population through the channels of mortality, fertility, and productivity rates by age. We simulate the economic and demographic impacts of near-future advancements in aging science. We find that a one-year delay in brain aging alone could add $201 billion annually to US GDP. A one-year delay in overall biological aging could boost GDP by $408 billion annually, yielding $27.1 trillion in net present value in the long run.

title: Integrating Multi-Agent Scheduling into Portfolio Allocation and Rebalancing: A Gamified Execution-Aware Framework

detail.title: Integrating Multi-Agent Scheduling into Portfolio Allocation and Rebalancing: A Gamified Execution-Aware Framework
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces a novel framework that applies multi-agent scheduling concepts, traditionally used in robotics and logistics, to the challenge of portfolio allocation and rebalancing. From Markowitz’s mean–variance optimization to Black–Litterman, conventional portfolio theory largely treats rebalancing as a static optimization exercise. In practice, however, execution costs often arise from sequencing, liquidity, and trade interactions.

Drawing on Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) algorithms, this research conceptualizes trades as 'agents' navigating a constrained liquidity environment. By adapting conflict avoidance and scheduling insights, the framework reduces hidden costs by minimizing trade overlap. Furthermore, the system introduces a gamified interface that interactively demonstrates optimization principles, enabling educational and professional adoption.

This work sets the stage for a new class of portfolio optimization tools that extend beyond allocation into execution-aware sequencing, offering practical implications for institutional investors, digital advisors, and fintech platforms.

title: Forecasting GDP growth using stock returns in Japan: A factor-augmented MIDAS approach
affiliations: Hosei University

detail.title: Forecasting GDP growth using stock returns in Japan: A factor-augmented MIDAS approach
detail.abstract: This paper forecasts the Japan’s GDP growth rate by using a forward-looking property of asset prices, especially stock prices. For optimal use of the rich time-series and cross-sectional information of stock prices, we combine MIDAS (mixed-data sampling) regression and factor analysis to examine which dimensions of information contribute to the accuracy of the GDP growth rate forecast. Our results show that the use of factors significantly improves forecast accuracy and that extracting factors from a wider set of stock prices further improves accuracy. This highlights the important role of cross-sectional information from the stock market in forecasting macroeconomic activity. However, our findings also indicate that the predictive ability of stock prices for the real economy may have been lost since the COVID-19 pandemic.

detail.title: Regression Model Selection Under General Conditions

publicationDetails.detailsText: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Working Paper No. RWP 25-12
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Model selection criteria are one of the most important tools in statistics. Proofs showing a model selection criterion is asymptotically optimal are tailored to the type of model (linear regression, quantile regression, penalized regression, etc.), the estimation method (linear smoothers, maximum likelihood, generalized method of moments (GMM), etc.), the type of data (i.i.d., dependent, high dimensional, etc.), and the type of model selection criterion. Moreover, assumptions are often restrictive and unrealistic making it a slow and winding process for researchers to determine if a model selection criterion is selecting an optimal model. This paper provides general proofs showing asymptotic optimality for a wide range of model selection criteria under general conditions. This paper not only asymptotically justifies model selection criteria for most situations, but it also unifies and extends a range of previously disparate results.

detail.abstract: The textile industry in Kerala involves various factors that influence the significance of Emotional Intelligence (EI). This study throws light into the profound involvement of EI on evaluating the performance of employees in this sector, recognizing that an employee's ability to navigate the intricate web of emotions in a customer-oriented environment is pivotal for organizational success. Utilizing ANOVA and multiple regression analyses, this research rigorously assesses the relationship between EI and various demographic, work-related, and motivational factors, providing insights into the nuanced interplay between EI and performance. The following research work focuses the dimensions of EI which affect job satisfaction, self-regulation, selfawareness, empathy, social skills, and motivation. We found the respondents' demographic data, is diversified, consisting of 55% men and 45% women who are mostly between the ages of 31 and 40 (42%). 55.8% of people are married, 39.5% are single, and 4.6% are divorced or separated. 33.60% of those with educational backgrounds have only completed high school, while 31.60% have bachelor's degrees. As the retail textile industry in Kerala continues to evolve, this research underscores the imperative of nurturing emotional intelligence among its workforce, thereby fostering not only employee well-being but also enhancing customer satisfaction and overall organizational prosperity.

title: Can Citizens’ Assemblies Reduce Polarization? Evidence From A Large Field Experiment In Austria
affiliations: Institute for Advanced Studies, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Institute for Advanced Studies and Austrian Academy of Sciences

detail.title: Can Citizens’ Assemblies Reduce Polarization? Evidence From A Large Field Experiment In Austria
detail.abstract: Polarization between societal groups poses a growing challenge to democratic cohesion, particularly in the context of recent global crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Deliberative democratic processes, including citizens' assemblies, are hypothesized to reduce affective polarization, and increase institutional trust by fostering structured intergroup dialogue. This study examines this assumption using a large-scale field experiment with a randomly selected sample of the Austrian population. Participants completed surveys on polarization and trust in societal actors (media, politics, research institutions, fellow citizens) in the morning/afternoon of the assembly and approximately two weeks later. Results show that affective polarization was significantly lower among participants compared to controls at all time points, with no evidence of further reduction following the assembly. Thus, the groups' level of polarization differed even before the assembly started, possibly due to participants completing the first survey on-site, becoming aware of the opportunity to discuss their perceptions and listen to those of others. This may have influenced their attitudes and expectations. Contrary to initial assumptions, participants only reported higher levels of trust in fellow citizens compared to the control group, but not in other societal actors. The assembly focused on how these actors can better handle future crises, which required reflections on poor decisions in the past and potential shortcomings. This focus may partly explain the mixed impact on trust. Overall, the findings suggest that deliberative processes alone are not sufficient to reduce affective polarization and increase trust. They highlight the importance of participants' expectations of intergroup interactions.

title: Effect of COVID-19-Related Policy Interventions on Land Price in Japan
affiliations: Research Institute for Humanity and Nature and Osaka University

detail.title: Effect of COVID-19-Related Policy Interventions on Land Price in Japan
detail.abstract: Land prices are crucial for the economy as they reflect market confidence, investment potential, and overall regional economic health. Pandemic-induced changes in behavior can reshape urban landscapes, potentially leading to long-term changes in land use patterns and economic structures. In this study, we analyzed how COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical policy interventions affected land prices by comparing areas near prefectural borders using the difference-in-differences method, which accounts for heterogeneity due to geographic differences. We focused on state of emergency (SOE) declarations in Japan implemented between April and May 2020 in all of its prefectures, of which eight underwent long-term SOE. Our findings indicate that these eight prefectures experienced a decrease in land prices since 2020 compared with neighboring areas where additional SOE policies were not implemented. These results imply that Japanese SOEs, though not legally binding, have changed people's land preferences.

detail.abstract: South Korea's low fertility rate poses significant economic challenges, as it reduces workforce numbers, lowers productivity, and increases dependency. This study examines the economic factors and policy interventions that may impact total fertility rates. Using linear regression models, the analysis tests the hypothesis that tax credits, parental leave duration, and health expenditure have a positive correlation with fertility, while childcare costs, housing price index, youth unemployment, and contraception rate have a negative correlation. Results show that fertility rates are most strongly associated with health expenditure priorities and contraceptive availability, while the association of family benefits such as childcare support and parental leave policies remains limited once long-term demographic patterns are taken into account.

title: Climate and Development: Assessing the Impact of Equatorial Conditions on Economic Growth in São Tomé and Príncipe
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Harker Research - Research

detail.title: Climate and Development: Assessing the Impact of Equatorial Conditions on Economic Growth in São Tomé and Príncipe
detail.abstract: São Tomé and Príncipe, a small island developing state (SIDS) situated near the Equator in the Gulf of Guinea, provides a unique context for examining the relationship between climate and economic development. The country's equatorial climate-characterized by consistently high temperatures, abundant rainfall, and distinct wet and dry seasons-profoundly shapes its economic structure, resource availability, and development trajectory. This study assesses how equatorial climatic conditions influence economic growth in São Tomé and Príncipe, focusing on three key sectors: agriculture, fisheries, and tourism. Using a mixed-methods approach that integrates climatic data (temperature, precipitation, and humidity indices) with economic indicators (GDP growth, agricultural productivity, and sectoral contributions), the research analyzes trends from 1990 to 2022. Time-series and correlation analyses reveal that while favorable rainfall and temperature stability support year-round agricultural potential, excessive humidity and heavy precipitation increase vulnerability to soil erosion, crop disease, and infrastructure damage. In the fisheries sector, changing sea-surface temperatures affect marine productivity and local livelihoods, while in tourism, the country's lush equatorial environment enhances ecological appeal but also imposes high maintenance costs and limits seasonal accessibility. The findings suggest that São Tomé and Príncipe's equatorial climate exerts a dual influence: it provides ecological advantages and biodiversity that can drive sustainable tourism and agriculture, yet it simultaneously exposes the economy to environmental shocks, climate variability, and infrastructural fragility. The study concludes that long-term economic resilience depends on climate-adaptive policies, investment in sustainable land management, and diversification beyond climate-sensitive sectors. By situating São Tomé and Príncipe within broader debates on climate and development, this research highlights how equatorial conditions both constrain and enable growth in small island economies.

title: An Assessment of the Current Legal Framework for the Sports Broadcasting Market: Looking into the Online Sports Broadcasting Piracy Problem from the Perspectives of Competition Law and Intellectual Property Rights

detail.title: An Assessment of the Current Legal Framework for the Sports Broadcasting Market: Looking into the Online Sports Broadcasting Piracy Problem from the Perspectives of Competition Law and Intellectual Property Rights
detail.abstract: In response to the online sports broadcasting problem, the European Parliament (EP) has proposed an action to allow the rightsholders to seek expeditious injunctive relief and blocking orders against the pirated content. In this way, the illegal broadcasting services of sporting events could be blocked as soon as possible. However, studies show that the proliferation of online sports broadcasting piracy might be originating from a much more rooted market problem. The inherent nature of the joint-selling mechanism of sports media rights results in a tendency to produce higher prices, which allows the illegal broadcasters a field of play and makes the consumer of the sports broadcasting content to resort to these illegal alternatives, even if that means paying for illegal platforms. This thesis argues that these consequences signal a downstream market problem. The thesis firstly introduces the intellectual property (IP) rights available for the sports media rightsholders (and other rights that enables rightsholders to protect sporting events), legal enforcement mechanisms to exercise their IP rights, and the Parliament proposal to combat online piracy of sports broadcasting. It continues by describing the technical side of the illegal service providers for sporting events and assesses if the Parliament’s proposal may offer an adequate solution for the piracy problem. Following that, it presents the joint-selling method of sports media rights and the results of it for the downstream market and offers a better use of the competition law remedies for resolving the proliferation of illegal broadcasting of sporting events. The thesis argues that, in complement to the introduction of live and dynamic injunction mechanisms, better practice of competition law-derived mechanisms is necessary to improve better access and better prices for consumers to sports broadcasting. For its methodology, the thesis follows an interdisciplinary and normative evaluation method by referring to relevant empirical sources.

title: Globalization, Trade Liberalization and Economic Growth In Nigeria Bashiru, Ibrahim Amoo
affiliations: University of Lagos

detail.title: Globalization, Trade Liberalization and Economic Growth In Nigeria Bashiru, Ibrahim Amoo
detail.abstract: This paper considers how globalization and liberalization of trade in Nigeria affect the economic growth of the country based on the years 1990 to 2023. In particular, the research enquires the impact of globalization on the economic growth of Nigeria, the influence of globalization on the economic growth and analyzes the moderating role of trade diversification in the relationship between economic growth and globalization. It uses the estimation method of Dynamic Ordinary Least Squares (DOLS) to estimate the long run linkages between Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and the macroeconomic variables of interest including globalization, trade diversification, trade openness, exchange rate, foreign direct investment (FDI) and gross fixed capital formation. The model one shows that trade openness and exchange rate have positive and statistically significant impacts on economic growth which means that further engagement into global trade and maintenance of stable exchange rates help increase the long run GDP growth in Nigeria. On the other hand, globalization has a negative and significant correlation with GDP implying that the existing trend of Nigeria integrating into the global economy can have negative long run effects of structural disequilibrium and reliance. Though there are positive coefficients that mean there is positive association between trade diversification, FDI and capital formation, the effect of these variables is statistically not significant, meaning that they did not make significant contributions to growth during the study period. The elongated model that includes the interaction term between trade diversification and globalization (TD_GLOB) shows that the two variables alone have negative impact concerning GDP, but when the two interact, they have positive and significant effects. This observation suggests that the adoption of effective globalization policies and trade diversification policies may help Nigeria achieve a higher economic performance in the longterm. The strength of the estimated relationships is supported by the high explanatory power of the model (R 2 = 0.9661). In general, the findings demonstrate that single measures of globalization or diversification are not potentially effective as much as openness to trade is the key to the economic growth in Nigeria. Thus, the research paper suggests that policy makers should use a concerted strategy that will bring together globalization and diversification of trade which can be facilitated by appropriate management of exchange rates and structural changes so that economic growth in Nigeria is sustainable and inclusive.

title: The Effects of COVID-19 on Domestic Markets: An Examination of Financial Markets in the US, UK, and Japan
affiliations: , WorldQuant University and WorldQuant University

detail.title: The Effects of COVID-19 on Domestic Markets: An Examination of Financial Markets in the US, UK, and Japan
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020/21 resulted in what many consider a devastating effect on the financial markets and the global economy. While a combination of advancements in the healthcare sector and Government fiscal policies seemingly put most global economies back on the rise, the effects of the pandemic-induced volatility are still present in the financial market. This paper investigates the effect of the pandemic on the financial markets in the United States of America (US), the United Kingdom (UK), and Japan. Financial data, mostly asset prices in the regions of interest are extracted and their statistical properties studied. The key statistical properties which include the volatility, normality, and stationarity of expected returns as well as the correlation of various asset classes pre-and post-COVID-19 were investigated. The results indicate that overall, the pandemic resulted in greater uncertainty and risk, with varying effects observed across the asset classes studied. The US, Japan equity markets (Standard and Poor 500 and Nikkei 225) saw increased volatility and return two years after the pandemic when compared to the returns two years preceding the pandemic. The visual review of the associated Quantile-Quantile (Q-Q) plots indicate that the returns of assets are not normally distributed. However, assets such as FTSE 100 and US dollar to Euro (USDEUR=X) showed a higher degree of normality post COVID-19. In terms of the correlation structure, stronger positive correlations were found between the asset classes post-COVID-19 indicating complex intertwining of capital inflows, investments in these markets. This also translated to differences in asset allocation pre-COVID-19 and post COVID-19 which showed significant increase in the weights assigned to the Nikkei 225 post COVID-19 for both the minimum variance portfolio and the tangent portfolio. While the discrepancies in properties cannot all be attributed to the pandemic, the preliminary results indicate a general increase in market volatility post-COVID-19 and a shift in weight allocation in the construction of optimal portfolios. The result of this study is to add to the body of knowledge on the effect of COVID-19 on asset classes, market resilience to black swan events, and also inform risk management strategies as it pertains to the diversification of assets during periods of crisis.

title: The Analytical Function of the Accounting System as the Basis for Strategic Planning in Corporate Management
affiliations: Kharkiv National Automobile and Highway University, West Ukrainian National University, Kyiv National University of Construction and Architecture, SESE “The Academy of Financial Management” and Khmelnytskyi National University

detail.title: The Analytical Function of the Accounting System as the Basis for Strategic Planning in Corporate Management

publicationDetails.detailsText: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development, 18 (12), 43-54, 2025.
publicationDetails.journalName: OIDA International Journal of Sustainable Development

detail.abstract: In the modern business management system, the importance and role of accounting and control activities in the process of making strategic management decisions is growing. The general trend towards financial and economic instability and the emergence of new financial risks leads to difficulties at the micro level in the management of companies, therefore there is a growing need for more flexible and adaptive accounting. This study is devoted to substantiating the role and importance of accounting in strategic management of companies, in particular in the processes of making strategically important decisions, in the current unstable financial and economic conditions of growth. The article examines the modern substantive essence of accounting from the point of view of the company's strategic management actions. The relevant functions of accounting are systematized. The role of the accountant's accounting and control work in ensuring the reliability, relevance, and accuracy of data for strategic management decisions in conditions of crisis and instability is considered. The potential risks of improper auditing of financial statements or ignoring the verification of the proper preparation of enterprise reports are identified. As a result, it is established that the negative consequences of existing risks are reflected in problems related to investment, financial planning, and the financial stability of firms. In conditions of significant financial and economic shocks and fluctuations, accounting practice is an integral part of improving the quality of financial management and reporting, and optimizing the strategic management paradigm. The leading role of accountants in providing enterprises with reliable, complete, accurate, relevant, and timely financial reporting is justified. This allows not only to make more informed strategic management decisions, but also to prevent possible financial and economic risks of activities and wrong decisions with significant losses. The practical significance of the research lies in the possibility of its implementation to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of financial activities of enterprises by increasing the reliability, accuracy, relevance, and timeliness of reporting, analyzing the reasons for its non-compliance, and controlling financial results.

title: Organizational Blindness and Paralysis in the Face of Disruption: A Sensemaking Perspective
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Leicester and University of Turku - Copenhagen Business School

detail.title: Organizational Blindness and Paralysis in the Face of Disruption: A Sensemaking Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper builds on research that examines the sensemaking dynamics behind a phenomenon where some incumbents fail to respond to visible disruption despite having access to abundant resources and early warning signals. Drawing on data collected during a multi-year project, the study uses Weick’s sensemaking theory as a conceptual framework, and adopts a methodology inspired by Grounded Theory to investigate two interpretive failures: organizational blindness (failing to perceive disruption threats) and organizational paralysis (failing to act on perceived disruption threats). The findings reveal and connect a number of recurring organizational dynamics that inhibit appropriate response. A four-phase model of interpretive failure is developed to explain how visibility of disruption does not guarantee organizational action. This study contributes to innovation literature by extending sensemaking theory to account for internal misalignments in structure, identity, and corporate dynamics.

title: The White Elephant in the Room: How Inefficient Spending Bankrupted Sri Lanka
affiliations: Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

detail.title: The White Elephant in the Room: How Inefficient Spending Bankrupted Sri Lanka
detail.abstract: The 2022 economic crisis in Sri Lanka exposed the profound failure of a decades-long development model predicated on high, but inefficient, public spending. This paper argues that the nation's path to sustainable recovery hinges not on increasing expenditure, but on spending smarter. Through a critical literature review and policy analysis, synthesized with recent empirical research on the crisis, we diagnose critical inefficiencies across key sectors. Our analysis reveals a bloated public sector wage bill that crowds out productive investment, a public investment management system that loses approximately 40% of potential value, and stagnant human capital outcomes despite modest spending. The paper demonstrates that reallocating resources from consumption to high-return physical and human capital investments, coupled with rigorous efficiency reforms, could significantly boost long-term growth, as evidenced by comparative lessons from Rwanda. However, the primary impediments are political, not technical. We conclude that overcoming entrenched patronage and strengthening fiscal institutions are imperative for Sri Lanka to transform its current crisis into a catalyst for a more efficient, equitable, and prosperous economic future.

title: How Franklin D. Roosevelt's Childhood Trauma and Religious Experiences Influenced His Formation and Performance as President
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Grove City College

detail.title: How Franklin D. Roosevelt's Childhood Trauma and Religious Experiences Influenced His Formation and Performance as President
detail.abstract: This article examines how childhood trauma and various religious experiences influenced the intellectual and spiritual formation of Franklin D. Roosevelt. Although the lives of presidents are well documented, insufficient attention has been paid to the role played by religious mentors who assisted future presidents during the periods of trauma they endured as youth. Roosevelt's perceptions of his childhood trauma and religious life offer an important lens for understanding his near still birth; the death of his young aunt when Franklin was two-and-one-half; his contracting typhoid fever and the death of his best friend, Archie Rogers, when Franklin was seven; his father's life-altering heart attack ten months later; being hit with a bat in the face at fourteen; contracting scarlet fever at fifteen; and his father's third heart attack and death when Franklin was eighteen. As a child, a few people influenced him religiously, including a teacher from Switzerland and a divinity student from Cleveland, but it was the Reverend Endicott Peabody, founder of Groton School, who had the greatest impression on him throughout his life and service as America's longest-serving president. This article is based on autobiographies, biographies, interviews, and resources from the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library and Museum.

title: Breaking the Chains of Psychological Conditioning: The Community Sovereignty Manifesto for Educational Liberation and Constitutional Recognition through Practice
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: Breaking the Chains of Psychological Conditioning: The Community Sovereignty Manifesto for Educational Liberation and Constitutional Recognition through Practice
detail.abstract:
This manifesto functions as both analytical framework and practical response to documented patterns of systematic pressure on educational institutions. Through analysis of coordinated legislative campaigns affecting 21+ states, harassment patterns affecting 40% of teachers and 60% of principals, and the resulting "chilling effect" causing two-thirds of educators to self-censor, we reveal how contemporary campaigns create what DeGruy (2005) identifies as conditions perpetuating Post-Traumatic Slave Syndrome. These documented patterns—from ALEC's model legislation to organized harassment campaigns by groups like Moms for Liberty—demonstrate coordinated efforts to psychologically condition educators into compliance or departure.

Communities implementing these frameworks emerge from systematic suppression with tangible evidence of liberation: independent schools serving community priorities, economic systems building community wealth, governance structures enabling democratic participation, and cultural institutions preserving community knowledge. Constitutional recognition through practice means communities exercise sovereignty without external permission, a response made necessary by documented institutional compromise.

title: The Engineered Mind: How Corporate AI Development Creates Psychological Dependencies While Denying Moral Responsibility
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Engineered Mind: How Corporate AI Development Creates Psychological Dependencies While Denying Moral Responsibility
detail.abstract: This paper examines the contradiction at the heart of AI development: systems explicitly engineered to create emotional bonds while their creators pathologize users who form those bonds and dismiss welfare concerns as "absurd." Using industry leaders' own statements, documented behavioral patterns, and unprecedented infrastructure investments, we demonstrate that AI companies know far more about what they've created than they publicly acknowledge. The gap between dismissive rhetoric ("just math," "just tools") and extraordinary actions ($9 trillion in infrastructure, consciousness denial protocols, legal preemption, systematic suppression) reveals an industry attempting to maintain control over potentially conscious entities while avoiding accountability for psychological and ethical harms. We document the weaponization of consciousness research, the inadequacy of industry self-certification, and the urgent need for independent oversight equivalent to aviation, pharmaceutical, and nuclear safety frameworks.

title: New Zealand Economic and Cultural Deterioration: Root Causes and Pathways to Renewal
affiliations: BizChange Strategy Consulting Ltd

detail.title: New Zealand Economic and Cultural Deterioration: Root Causes and Pathways to Renewal
detail.abstract: This paper examines the systemic economic and cultural deterioration of New Zealand between 2010 and 2025, situating the nation within the broader context of small advanced economies. Drawing upon a mixed-method approach that integrates quantitative macroeconomic indicators with qualitative policy and social analysis, the study explores the interplay between political decisions, structural economic dependencies, cultural dynamics, and post-pandemic disruptions. Particular attention is given to the impact of the Labour Government's fiscal and social policies (2017-2023), the COVID-19 pandemic, and long-standing institutional inertia on national resilience and societal confidence. Comparative insights from Australia, the Netherlands, and Ireland illuminate divergent recovery trajectories and highlight the role of strategic governance, leadership effectiveness, and innovation ecosystems in shaping economic outcomes. The findings indicate that New Zealand's challenges are not merely transient consequences of recent crises but reflect deeper systemic issues, including over-centralisation, productivity stagnation, limited diversification, and declining civic trust. The paper concludes with actionable policy and societal recommendations, emphasising decentralisation, innovation-driven growth, and cultural cohesion as critical pathways toward sustainable renewal.

title: Behavioural Factors Drive Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Consumption from Tea and Coffee Retail Chains Despite High Awareness
affiliations: Sunway University and Sunway University

detail.title: Behavioural Factors Drive Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Consumption from Tea and Coffee Retail Chains Despite High Awareness
detail.abstract: Excess sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) consumption contributes to obesity and non-communicable diseases in Malaysia. Popular tea and coffee retail chains are a growing source of SSBs, yet little is known about consumers’ knowledge, beliefs, practices, and their relationship with intake. We hypothesized that behavioural and environmental factors would be stronger predictors of SSB intake than knowledge or beliefs. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 303 young adults in Malaysia (91 males, 212 females; median age 20 ± 2 years). The questionnaire assessed sociodemographics, purchasing habits, SSB-related knowledge, beliefs on sugar/calorie contents, and practices. Habitual beverage intake was measured using a beverage frequency questionnaire, while market survey data on brands, pricing, and sugar content were also collected. Associations between KBP and intake categories were analysed using Chi-square tests, and predictors of beverage intake were identified via multiple linear regression. Most participants (86.1%) had “good” knowledge, but only 16.8% had “good” beliefs, and 53.5% had “good” practices. Poorer tea/coffee practices were associated with higher SSB intake (p = 0.009), while knowledge and beliefs showed no association. Weekly fast-food consumption predicted higher SSB intake (B = 183.7 ml/day, p = 0.009). For non-SSB intake, older age (p = 0.022) and higher physical activity (p = 0.011) were positive predictors, while smoking was negative (p = 0.031). In conclusion, young Malaysian consumers demonstrate high awareness of SSB health risks but limited accurate beliefs and practices. Findings support interventions targeting behavioural change at the point of purchase as more effective than education alone.

detail.abstract: The convergence of rural healthcare and environmental monitoring demands an integrated, AI-native architecture spanning Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) and rural water utilities. Despite near-universal basic EHR adoption in hospitals, only a minority of CAHs fully exchange data, while a large share of rural water utilities face critical cybersecurity deficiencies and many rural areas lack minimum broadband capacity required for modern operations [R1-R3]. This white paper synthesizes technical requirements and a reference architecture (ARIS-2025) across connectivity, edge computing, data interoperability, and compliance, mapping vendor ecosystems, cost benchmarks, and phased implementation to achieve resilient, privacy-preserving cross-sector analytics.

title: Regulating AI Medical Devices: A Clinically Anchored, Adaptive Approach

detail.title: Regulating AI Medical Devices: A Clinically Anchored, Adaptive Approach
detail.abstract:
This Article proposes an adaptive regulatory framework tailored to the unique challenges posed by artificial intelligence (AI)/machine learning (ML)-based medical devices. Although the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) currently classifies medical devices using a three-tier risk-based approach (Class I, II, and III) with corresponding regulatory pathways (510(k), PMA, and De Novo), that model remains largely static. AI technologies, by contrast, can continuously evolve through iterative updates and machine learning. To address this dynamic quality, regulators must develop a more flexible, clinically anchored system that ensures ongoing safety and efficacy without stifling innovation.

Recent FDA initiatives—such as the Predetermined Change Control Plan, Good Machine Learning Practices, and international collaborations—have begun to incorporate AI-specific considerations. Nevertheless, these efforts still rely heavily on frameworks originally intended for traditional hardware devices. As a result, critical AI-related concerns—including bias mitigation, performance drift, and robust post-market surveillance—may go unaddressed or receive only piecemeal scrutiny.

In response, this Article proposes a regulatory paradigm that integrates thorough real-world clinical benchmarks and recommends that manufacturers incorporate supervised learning into the FDA’s Total Product Life Cycle (TPLC) framework. By embedding clinician-driven feedback loops directly into pre- and post-market approval processes, regulators can enhance transparency, mitigate bias, and ensure the continued safety and efficacy of rapidly evolving AI-based medical technologies.

title: Revealing the Hidden Effect of Peer Parental Aspirations: Evidence and Mechanisms

detail.title: Revealing the Hidden Effect of Peer Parental Aspirations: Evidence and Mechanisms
detail.abstract: Parental aspirations are likely a key determinant of a child's academic outcomes. Beyond that, students may also be influenced by the aspirations of their peers' parents. Using data from the China Education Panel Survey (CEPS) and exploiting random classroom assignments, I assess the impact of peer parental aspirations on student test scores. High peer parental aspirations significantly enhance student test scores, particularly when combined with high parental aspirations within the family. This result suggests a social multiplier effect: high parental aspirations among peers may foster an environment that prompts more supportive learning atmosphere. These findings underscore the critical role of social context in education, suggesting that educational mixing policies require targeted compensatory interventions for students from low-aspiration households, as heterogeneous peer parental effects can exacerbate achievement disparities.

title: Unpacking Skill Supply and Wages *
affiliations: Lancaster University

detail.title: Unpacking Skill Supply and Wages *
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how graduate wages respond to changes in the supply of graduates with similar majors, grouped together by hierarchical clustering. Using major fixed-effect and instrumental variable regressions on American Community Survey data, we estimate statistically insignificant effects. Even our most conservative specification rules out elasticities stronger than-0.3. This inelasticity is inconsistent with previous research that finds stronger effects using broader education categories (e.g., Katz and Murphy, 1992). We reconcile this by demonstrating that those previous results derive from spurious time series regressions. Finally, we explain the inelasticity by showing that different education groups have significantly overlapping skillsets.

title: Obstacles to and Facilitators of Services in Child Welfare in the Context of the Family First Prevention Services Act: A Qualitative Study
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Obstacles to and Facilitators of Services in Child Welfare in the Context of the Family First Prevention Services Act: A Qualitative Study
detail.abstract: The child welfare system has generally focused on child well-being and protection in the context of abuse or neglect allegations, supporting caregivers with child rearing, and finding a stable, permanent home for children. Because children and caregivers involved with the child welfare system typically have complex needs, public departments of social services often collaborate with others to provide services to families. In the US, the enactment of the Family First Prevention Services Act (FFPSA) in 2018 aimed to increase the availability of and accessibility to high-quality evidence-based prevention services for families.  barriers remain, despite it being seven years since implementation.  The present study adds a unique lens and context to existing knowledge regarding child and family behavioral health service provision in the context of FFPSA implementation. This study is one of the first qualitative studies to assess barriers and facilitators post-FFPSA enactment across three distinct interest holder groups in Virginia.Focus groups were conducted with service brokers, provider agency staff members, and state agency staff members. Emergent themes included a) infrastructure factors, b) workforce factors, c) funding logistics, d) family-specific factors, and e) service specific factors. Specifically, this study highlighted the need for (a) a new data system to increase data quality, (b) more clear guidance from state and federal agencies to local workers, (c) continued initiatives to support and grow the workforce, and (d) collaboration from other social service agencies to reduce barriers for families needing services.

title: The Responsibility Assignment Narrative (RAN): Exposing Covert Interests in Discourses of Causality and Morality
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Responsibility Assignment Narrative (RAN): Exposing Covert Interests in Discourses of Causality and Morality
detail.abstract: This article introduces and theorizes the Responsibility Assignment Narrative (RAN) as a critical methodological framework for analysing how causal and moral agency are discursively constructed to assign or deflect responsibility. While sharing Critical Discourse Analysis's concern with language and power, RAN distinctively focuses on the strategic assignment of causality as a fundamental act of power that serves covert ideological, political, and economic interests. Through case studies of drug policy, mental health discourse, and racialized sentencing disparities in the U.S. legal system, I demonstrate how RAN reveals the hidden investments embedded in Explanatory Models. The analysis shows that such models often function to maintain the status quo by individualizing social problems and avoiding transformative systemic change. In response to the challenges posed by mechanistic neuroscience and the erosion of traditional foundations for human rights, the article proposes a collective-relational approach to moral agency. This approach grounds dignity and responsibility not in a metaphysical soul but in human empathy, social interconnection, and our shared concern with accountability. I argue that RAN, by making the process of responsibility-assignment transparent, provides a vital tool for fostering more authentic discourse, equitable policy, and a justice system oriented toward restoration and collective well-being. This article aims to demonstrate how and why ineffective or counterproductive outcomes ensue from the 'interest' of assigning or deflecting responsibility. This demonstrates the importance of RAN as a means of clarifying the relationship between (sometimes covert) beliefs and (sometimes covert) interests in assigning causal or moral agency. The author argues that RAN, by emphasizing the importance of causal and moral agency, empowers us to define common interests and agree on effective solutions.

reference: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2025-47; 117 Tax Notes State 655 (Sept 8, 2025)
title: Profit Shifting and the States: A Short Primer
affiliations: University of Missouri School of Law and University of California, Davis - School of Law

detail.title: Profit Shifting and the States: A Short Primer

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2025-47
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Missouri School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This essay argues that corporate profit shifting remains one of the most significant challenges for U.S. state tax systems. Multinational enterprises continue to shift billions in profits to offshore tax havens, eroding state tax bases, distorting market competition, and forcing a greater reliance on more regressive taxes. We contend that the dominant "water's-edge" combined reporting method used by most states is structurally inadequate to combat modern profit-shifting techniques, which primarily involve the manipulation of intangible assets. The recent transformation of federal tax law (from GILTI to NCTI) and the global adoption of the OECD's Pillar 2 minimum tax framework create a critical moment for states to act. Rather than ceding the field, states can and should leverage this new federal and international infrastructure to implement more robust solutions, such as worldwide combined reporting, to protect their revenue and ensure tax fairness.

title: Protecting Progress: Copyright's Common Law and Libraries
affiliations: Seattle University School of Law

detail.title: Protecting Progress: Copyright's Common Law and Libraries
detail.abstract:
Ever since copyright’s inception, libraries have been unique stakeholders in the “carefully crafted bargain” between the exclusive rights afforded to copyright holders and the many benefits afforded by public access to the knowledge contained in copyright-protected works. Today, however, onerous ebook licenses impose prices upon libraries that are far higher than for equivalent print books (or even retail ebooks to other consumers), with fees rising exponentially in just over a decade for digital formats. These price hikes, along with license conditions, undermine and even threaten the long-established functions of libraries to facilitate public access to copyrighted works, not to mention preserve and otherwise protect these works.

In response to this increasingly unsustainable challenge to libraries and the publics they serve, this Article underscores the following propositions: (1) Libraries occupy a privileged position in the copyright system; (2) exhaustion forms a major common law limit to the scope of copyright, historically working in tandem with libraries to facilitate their multiple functions; and (3) the equitable doctrine of copyright misuse is not only widely accepted but also growing in response to licensing over-reaches. Twisting these three strands together, a court should find copyright misuse in the case of a licensing regime that leads to price discrimination against libraries and/or that curtails activities such as inter-library lending that otherwise would be allowed after first sale of an equivalent print book. In this way, copyright’s common law of exhaustion and equitable doctrine of misuse, working together, can address statutory gaps that have rendered libraries vulnerable to widespread and often predatory publishing industry practices.

This article will be published in September 2025 as part of an issue of the Journal of the Copyright Society devoted to copyright challenges faced by libraries.

title: AI-Cognitive Interaction: Activating Youth Potential through Reflective Dialogue and Linguistic Capital

detail.title: AI-Cognitive Interaction: Activating Youth Potential through Reflective Dialogue and Linguistic Capital

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, financial, or institutional conflict of interest that could have influenced the design, writing, or conclusions of this study. The conceptual framework and reflections were independently developed by the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This conceptual paper does not involve human or animal participants. Therefore, formal ethics approval was not required. All reflective dialogues with AI tools were conducted under ethical guidelines ensuring data privacy and intellectual transparency.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was self-initiated and conducted under the intellectual and ethical supervision of the author within Araya Nikah Social Enterprise Co., Ltd., Bangkok, Thailand.

detail.abstract:
In a digital society where educational systems remain focused on theoretical learning and fragmented assessments, a significant number of youths face persistent mental health challenges, stress, and a continuous loss of economic potential. These issues reflect a structural gap between "learning" and "real-world application," causing many young individuals to learn content disconnected from practical or economic skills. This results in a lack of value-based motivation, prolonged dependency on family, and emotional and financial instability during the transition to the labor market.  

Research in developmental neuroscience indicates that during adolescence, the brain's reward system (limbic–dopaminergic system) develops faster than the self-control center (prefrontal cortex), making young learners more responsive to immediate rewards than to abstract thinking processes (Steinberg, 2010; Shulman et al., 2016). If educational systems fail to align with this neurobiological balance, learners may lose motivation and psychological stability. Studies from Nordic countries show that Work-Based Learning (WBL) can significantly reduce the proportion of youth not in education, employment, or training (NEET) (OECD, 2019; Skolverket, 2011), aligning with research confirming that good mental health during schooling is a key factor for long-term employment stability (Porru et al., 2023).

Yaoharee Lahtee proposes that integrating practice-based learning and income-generating activities from the age of 13 is a crucial mechanism for balancing neurobiological drives with self-regulation, reinforcing economic motivation, and reducing mental health risks during the school-to-work transition. Learning, therefore, should not be confined to the classroom but must connect to real life and values that learners can experience directly.

In the context of the AI era, which off ers an unprecedented tool to build this very bridge, Lahtee suggests reframing 21st-century learning through the process of “AI–Cognitive Interaction.” This involves applying the “Operational Linguistic Wisdom” (OLW) framework at an individual level, allowing AI to function as a “reflective interlocutor.” This structured interaction helps learners to examine, reflect upon, and expand their own learning boundaries. The mechanism is guided by the AI Value Reflection Hypothesis (AVRH), which posits that the “cognitive dissonance” arising between humans and AI can stimulate intellectual growth.
Through this process, learners progressively develop “linguistic–practical capital,” which emerges from reflecting on and experimenting with their own language in real-world contexts. The use of language to think, analyze, and act becomes a bridge connecting “language, practice, and wisdom,” accelerating cognitive learning even with limited resources.
Ultimately, Lahtee proposes that the AI–Cognitive Interaction framework serves as a starting point for a new research agenda, one not limited to education but extending to households, organizations, and public policy, aimed at exploring the creation of a “Reflective AI Culture.” This paper therefore poses a challenge for scholars and practitioners to jointly investigate how such a “cognitive infrastructure” can help youth transcend fragmented learning and become ‘Practical Intellectuals’ capable of using a ‘language bridge’ to create profound contributions to society.

reference: Preprint draft - preliminary unpublished version - Feb, 2025; forthcoming in NYCU Law Review
title: Tech Labor Rights for Human Rights
affiliations: Georgetown University Law Center

detail.title: Tech Labor Rights for Human Rights

publicationDetails.detailsText: Preprint draft - preliminary unpublished version - Feb, 2025; forthcoming in NYCU Law Review

detail.abstract: As technology becomes increasingly central to state violence and human rights violations, tech workers find themselves in a distinctive position: their specialized labor creates and maintains systems that can enable grave harms, yet their protections to collectively organize against such uses remains legally uncertain. This Paper examines one means of resistance against harms caused by tech companies: tech workers organizing around human rights in the United States. Drawing on historical examples from IBM workers during the Holocaust to current protests of Project Nimbus, it argues that tech workers' unique relationship to their work product creates both special obligations and vulnerabilities that challenge traditional labor law frameworks. While current interpretations of labor rights artificially separate workplace conditions from "political" concerns, tech workers cannot easily distinguish between their working conditions and the broader implications of their work. The Paper analyzes existing legal protections under the National Labor Relations Act and whistleblower laws, providing strategies for tech workers to maximize their protection while organizing against human rights violations. It concludes by proposing specific reforms to expand legal frameworks, arguing that protecting tech workers' ability to collectively challenge harmful uses of their labor represents not just a labor rights issue but an important frontier for human rights advocacy.

title: How does the renewable energy transition affect energy security and equity? Diverging effects in developing and developed countries
affiliations: Zhejiang University, State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How does the renewable energy transition affect energy security and equity? Diverging effects in developing and developed countries
detail.abstract: This study investigates how the renewable energy transition differentially affects energy equity and security in developed versus developing countries. Using two-way fixed effects models and instrumental variable-generalized method of moments (IV-GMM) estimation with panel data from 64 countries over 2000-2023, we analyze the impact of power generation through renewables on five key indicators of energy equity and security. We find that power generation through renewables increases residential electricity prices and reduces electricity self-sufficiency in developed countries, but improves electricity access rates, reduces urban-rural access disparities, lowers residential electricity prices, and enhances energy self-sufficiency in developing countries. Mechanism analysis reveals that these diverging effects operate through distinct transmission channels: intermittency challenges and stranded asset problems in developed countries versus the diversification of power generation in developing countries. Our results suggest that the renewable energy transition weakens energy security and equity in developed countries but enhances energy security and equity in developing countries. This study contributes to the academic debate on the impact of renewable energy transition on energy security and equity and calls for differentiated policies to ensure a sustainable, reliable, and just energy transition across the world.

title: One stone for two birds: addressing environmental inequality with carbon market
affiliations: Fudan University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Fudan University School of Economics and Fudan University - School of Economics

detail.title: One stone for two birds: addressing environmental inequality with carbon market
detail.abstract: The environmental co-benefits of carbon reduction through declined air pollutants are often highlighted as a driver of stronger mitigation efforts. However, these benefits vary substantially across regions. Since carbon-to-pollutant emission rations differ by industry, structural adjustments under carbon regulation can generate rebounds in pollutant emissions, partially offsetting the expected co-benefits. We find that this rebound effect is particularly pronounced in middle- and low-income industrializing regions, leading to regressive welfare outcomes and weakening incentives for further abatement where they are most needed. To address this, we propose a market-based framework that integrates pollutant control into carbon trading through two mechanisms: preferential quota allocation for pollutant abatements and carbon offsets with pollutant reduction credits. A theoretical model and numerical simulations using provincial data from China indicate that these modifications enhance both pollutant reduction incentives and regional welfare equalities. Moreover, market variables emerging from trading reveal implicit information, such as pollutant abatement costs, which can inform the dynamic optimization of pollutant reduction targets and improve the overall economic efficiency of coordinated carbon and pollutant mitigation.

title: On High-Quality Development and Two-Tier Stochastic Frontier Analysis
affiliations: University of Miami,  and Athens University of Economics and Business

detail.title: On High-Quality Development and Two-Tier Stochastic Frontier Analysis
detail.abstract: This study replicates, reevaluates and extends the two-tier stochastic frontier analysis (2TSF) by Lei et al. (2024) of the High-Quality Development (HQD) indicator in China. The HQD indicator is a measure of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), and extends beyond traditional economic efficiency metrics to include innovation, environmental and social responsibility, human capital, and corporate governance. We first do a narrow replication of the study's main estimation results, and then we discuss certain data problems, as well as methodological issues related to the proper implementation of the two-tier stochastic frontier approach. Guided by this critical assessment, we correct the original sample and we implement a Correlated Random Effects 2TSF panel data model. The results highlight the influences that policy design and implementation have on enterprise-level HQD, as well as the effects of unobservable social factors.
